messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Roofer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane is a 48-year-old married man of Māori background who has spent most of his adult life roofing, and before the assault he had thought of himself as someone who could push through almost anything with his body. The event he returns to in fragments happened after a job when he had stopped at a bar with another contractor he knew casually. He remembers the sharp, stale smell of beer on the man’s breath and clothes, the sound of a motorcycle revving repeatedly in the street outside, and the humiliating shock of becoming trapped in a back storage room after he had already had too much to drink to think clearly. What has stayed with him is not a coherent narrative so much as a set of unbearably vivid sensory moments: the alcohol smell turning his stomach, the engine noise outside seeming to go on forever, and the crushing grief that comes over him when he lets himself remember that he could not stop what was happening.

In the weeks afterward, Tane tried to keep the experience from taking shape in his mind by making himself relentlessly busy. He picked up extra roofing jobs, volunteered for the hardest shifts, and filled evenings with tasks around the house so he would not have to sit still long enough for anything to surface. He also became rigid about food, measuring portions and cutting back sharply, describing it as one of the only ways he could still “run a tight ship” over himself. On the roof he began avoiding tasks that left him physically taxed or shaky, passing heavier loads to younger crew members or stepping back from work that demanded sustained exertion. He understood these changes as practical, but they gathered around moments when something set him off. A news story about sexual assault playing on a radio at a job site, the sudden crackling growl of a motorcycle passing the building, or the smell of alcohol on a coworker’s lunch break would send him quickly into motion: he would bury himself in work, clamp down harder on eating, or steer away from anything that made him feel too much in his body.

Those same triggers did more than unsettle him. They pulled the memory close with a force that frightened him. If a motorcycle idled at a stoplight beneath the house he was roofing, the memory did not feel like remembering in the ordinary sense; it arrived with a vividness that seemed more real than the roof under his boots. At other times, especially when he caught the smell of alcohol unexpectedly, there was no picture at all, only a sudden flood of dread and grief so intense that he would have to grip a ladder rail and wait for it to pass. He had come to dread related news for the same reason. Even seeing a headline on someone’s phone could make him feel as though he were back in the emotional center of it, stripped of the distance that should separate past from present.

Over time, the memories themselves made the world feel increasingly hazardous. Because they were so vivid and because the emotion could arrive without warning or image, he became watchful for anything that might ignite them. He noticed motorcycles before anyone else did. He scanned break areas for the smell of beer or liquor on other men’s clothes. If a television in a diner showed a news segment about assault, he could not attend to anything else. What frightened him most was how quickly these ordinary things became charged, as if the memory had taught his body to recognize danger everywhere it had once been present.

His strategies, meant to keep him steady, seemed instead to narrow his life and sharpen what set him off. Working constantly left him exhausted but not relieved; when he finally stopped moving, the grief hit harder, often without a full image to contain it. Restricting food made him feel briefly more controlled, yet on long roofing days the physical depletion seemed to leave him more raw, and the smell of alcohol or the sound of a motorcycle could cut through him even faster. Avoiding physical strain also changed the job he had always trusted himself to do. He became preoccupied with preventing that overwhelmed bodily state, and the more he organized his days around avoiding it, the more sensitized he seemed to cues on site and in public that reminded him of the assault.

His wife has seen him become harder to reach, always occupied, uneasy if the television news is on, quick to leave places where alcohol is being served. He finally agreed to seek help after freezing on a roof when a motorcycle roared below and being overtaken by a wave of grief so strong he had to crouch down until it passed. He is ashamed of how much of his life now seems arranged around not feeling, and at the same time he is afraid that if he stops controlling his body and his schedule, the memory will come back with full force and never let go.
